about: CK-F, the Foundations checkpoint: nine short tasks on unfamiliar situations across T0-T6 and N1, then the main estimate (a town's school buses go electric). Prairie Town is fictional; its numbers are illustrative. The two charts use real Southwest Power Pool shapes (EIA-930, 2025) scaled to Prairie Town as in lesson 0 (450 MW = SPP's 2025 peak hour); the course's tests check them against town_year.json and town_days.json, and check every answer below.

tasks.title: Why balance every moment?
tasks.prompt: In one or two sentences: why must supply equal demand at every moment on a power grid, and what tells the operator when it does not?
points: The grid stores almost no energy, so power is made as it is used; only the spinning machines' stored energy covers a gap, for seconds.
The frequency shows a gap: a shortfall makes it fall below 60 Hz and a surplus makes it rise; controls then restore the balance and bring it back to 60 Hz.
tasks.solution: Power is made as it is used; only the spinning machines' stored energy covers a gap, for seconds. A shortfall makes the frequency fall, a surplus makes it rise, and controls then restore the balance and 60 Hz.

tasks.title: Phone charges in a day
tasks.prompt: A U.S. home uses about 10,800 kWh of electricity a year. A phone takes about 15 Wh for a full charge (illustrative). About how many full charges equal one day of the home's use?

why.a: That forgets that 1 kWh is 1,000 Wh.
why.b: That is one hour of the home's use, not a day.
why.c: One day is about 30 kWh, or 30,000 Wh.
why.d: That is a whole year, not one day.

tasks.solution: One day: 10,800 kWh ÷ 365 ≈ 30 kWh = 30,000 Wh, and 30,000 Wh ÷ 15 Wh ≈ 2,000 charges. The trap is the k: kWh and Wh differ by a factor of 1,000.

tasks.title: A December day's demand
tasks.prompt: The chart shows Prairie Town's demand on a real December weekday. When is demand highest, and how much above the day's lowest hour?
options: 07:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour
19:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour
14:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour

why.b: The axis starts at 260 MW, not zero, so the line exaggerates the swing.
why.c: 19:00 is the evening hump, lower than the morning peak.

tasks.solution: Peak 347 MW at 07:00, low 282 MW at 14:00 and 15:00: 347 ÷ 282 ≈ 1.23, about a quarter higher. Always read where the axis starts, here at 260 MW, not zero.

tasks.title: After a plant trips
tasks.prompt: A 60 MW gas unit in Prairie Town's region trips (shuts down suddenly). Put what happens next in order, first at the top.
items: The frequency starts to fall below 60 Hz; the spinning machines' stored energy covers the gap for a moment.
Within seconds, governors (automatic speed controls on running plants) raise output and the fall stops.
Within minutes, the operator's control system orders reserve plants (spare capacity kept ready) up to replace the lost 60 MW.
The frequency is back at 60 Hz, and the operator restores its reserves for the next trip.
tasks.solution: The frequency falls first; governors stop the fall within seconds but leave it below 60 Hz. Reserves replace the lost power over minutes and bring 60 Hz back; only then are the reserves rebuilt.

tasks.title: Forecast against actual
tasks.prompt: The chart shows the day-ahead forecast and the actual demand of a real spring day, scaled to Prairie Town. Over the day, the forecast was mostly…
options: too low, by at most about 2% of demand
too high, by at most about 2% of demand
too low, by up to about 20% of demand

why.a: Actual demand sits above the forecast in most hours, by at most 6 MW.
why.b: Look at which line is on top: actual demand is above the forecast.
why.c: The largest gap is 6 MW on about 290 MW: about 2%.
why.d: The two lines differ in most hours.

tasks.solution: Actual demand is above the forecast in 19 of 24 hours; the largest miss is 6 MW at 13:00 and 14:00, about 2% of demand. Operators hold reserves to cover misses like these.

tasks.title: A wind farm's year
tasks.prompt: A 50 MW wind farm runs at the 2025 U.S. average capacity factor for wind, 33.8%. About how much energy does it make in a year?
tasks.solution: 50 MW × 8,760 h × 0.338 ≈ 148,000 MWh, or 148 GWh. Without the capacity factor you would get 438,000 MWh: the farm at full output every hour, which no wind farm does.

tasks.title: A windless winter evening
tasks.prompt: A windless winter evening at 18:00, with demand near its peak. Assume every plant is available and has fuel. Which pair can Prairie Town count on?
options: The solar farm and the wind farm
The gas peaker and the nuclear plant
The wind farm and the nuclear plant
Rooftop solar and the gas peaker

why.a: The sun is down and the wind is calm.
why.b: Neither depends on sun or wind: available and fuelled, both can run, within their operating limits.
why.c: The wind is calm, so the wind farm makes almost nothing.
why.d: The sun is down at 18:00 in winter.

tasks.solution: Firm capacity is output you can count on when it is needed. At a calm winter dusk, with plants available and fuelled, that is the gas peaker and the nuclear plant; wind and solar do other jobs.

tasks.title: Spot the error in a headline
tasks.prompt: Made-up headline: “New 100 MW solar farm will power 100,000 homes.” At the 2025 U.S. solar capacity factor (24.0%) and 10,800 kWh per home a year, about how many homes' yearly use does it make?

why.a: Too few: check the hours in a year, 8,760.
why.b: About 210,000 MWh a year, divided by 10.8 MWh per home.
why.c: That is the headline. Even at full output every hour, the farm would make only about 81,000 homes' yearly use.
why.d: That is ten times too many: check MW against kW.

tasks.solution: 100 MW × 8,760 h × 0.240 ≈ 210,000 MWh a year, or about 19,500 homes at 10.8 MWh each. Even nameplate (maximum rated) output every hour would make only about 81,000: the headline fails the physics question.

tasks.prompt: Prairie Town's 20 diesel school buses go electric. Estimate the electricity they will use in a year, stating your assumptions. The fields below ask for a range with units, the main uncertainty and one way to check.
